title: btw_mcp_server() errors at startup when `tools` is a character vector of length > 1
description:
`btw_mcp_server()` opens by testing whether its `tools` argument names an R file:

https://github.com/posit-dev/btw/blob/main/R/mcp.R#L165-L172

```r
is_likely_r_file <-
  is.character(tools) &&
  file.exists(tools) &&
  grepl("[.]r$", tools, ignore.case = TRUE)
```

Since R 4.3, an `&&` whose operand has length > 1 is an error rather than a warning. So if `tools` is a character vector naming two or more tool groups, `file.exists(tools)` returns a length-*n* logical and the call dies immediately:

```r
btw::btw_mcp_server(c("docs", "env", "sessioninfo"))
#> Error in is.character(tools) && file.exists(tools) :
#>   'length = 3' in coercion to 'logical(1)'
```

A length-1 character vector is fine (`file.exists("docs")` is `FALSE`, so the guard short-circuits), which makes the failure look arbitrary — `btw_mcp_server("docs")` works, adding one more group breaks it.

Nothing else in the function objects to a character vector. The guard is the only obstacle; `flatten_and_check_tools()` handles one happily:

```r
length(btw:::flatten_and_check_tools(c("docs", "env", "ide")))
#> [1] 8
```

### Why this is worse than an ordinary error

The intended use is as an MCP server behind `Rscript -e`, where nothing has a terminal. The process dies before the `initialize` handshake, so the client sees only a closed pipe and reports a generic transport failure — Claude Code shows `Failed to reconnect to r-btw: -32000` — while the R message goes nowhere. There is no indication that the argument is at fault, or even that R produced an error. It took reconstructing the `Rscript` invocation by hand and running it in a terminal to see the real message.

### Suggested fix

Guard the length, e.g.

```r
is_likely_r_file <-
  is.character(tools) &&
  length(tools) == 1 &&
  file.exists(tools) &&
  grepl("[.]r$", tools, ignore.case = TRUE)
```

which also matches the intent, since the file branch only makes sense for a single path. If a character vector is meant to be rejected rather than accepted, an explicit error naming `tools` would still be a large improvement over the coercion message.

### Workaround

Wrap the groups so `is.character()` is `FALSE` — either `btw_mcp_server(btw_tools("docs", "env", "sessioninfo"))` or the `list(...)` form the docs use.

### A documentation note

Every example in `?btw_mcp_server` passes `list(...)` or `btw_tools(...)`, so the docs are consistent and correct. But `c(...)` is a natural thing to reach for, it is what a character-vector-shaped argument invites, and the rest of the function supports it — so people will hit this. Rejecting it loudly or accepting it both seem better than the current behaviour.

### Session info

```
R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24)
btw 1.3.0
```

title: How do I deploy btw-generated skills to a package user?
description:
I'm building an R package (<https://github.com/AlgoCompSynth/eikosany>) that includes a `btw` Shiny chat agent to answer questions from a user about using the package and carry out tasks requested by the user. Note that the user would see the package as installed, not as I see it as the developer or as you'd see it in the GitHub source repository.

To make the chat agent's question answering easier, I'm adding skills with `btw::btw_task_create_skill`. `btw` placed them in a directory `.btw/skills` in the root of the package as seen by the developer. `devtools::check()` does not like that for two reasons:

1. It's a non-standard file in the root of the package directory, and
2. It's a "hidden" file (name starts with a `.`).

I've moved the directory to `inst/btw`, which satisfies `devtools::check()` and means the skills will be in the package both for me as the developer and a user who's installed it. But will the chat agent be able to find them?

title: Add patch-style file editing tool
description:
# Patch Tool Implementation Spec

## 1. Purpose

Implement a structured patch tool for agentic file editing. The tool must support multi-file file operations using a patch envelope and diff-like update hunks.

The implementation should be deterministic, safe, and easy for language models to produce.

## 2. Supported Operations

The patch format must support these operations:

* `Add File`
* `Update File`
* `Delete File`
* `Move to` optional, as part of an update

## 3. Wire Format

### 3.1 Envelope

All patch input must be wrapped in:

```text
*** Begin Patch
...operations...
*** End Patch
```

### 3.2 Operation Headers

Each operation begins with exactly one of:

```text
*** Add File: <path>
*** Update File: <path>
*** Delete File: <path>
```

For renames/moves during update:

```text
*** Move to: <path>
```

### 3.3 Path Rules

* Paths are relative to the workspace root.
* Paths must be normalized before use.
* Reject any path that escapes the workspace root.
* Reject absolute paths unless explicitly allowed by policy.
* Reject empty paths.

## 4. Add File Syntax

### 4.1 Format

```text
*** Add File: docs/example.md
+Hello
+World
```

### 4.2 Semantics

* Create a new file at the target path.
* File contents are the concatenation of all lines after stripping the leading `+`.
* Preserve line order exactly.
* Empty files are allowed.

### 4.3 Validation

* Reject if file already exists, unless overwrite is explicitly supported by policy.
* Reject if any non-empty body line does not begin with `+`.
* Reject malformed headers.

## 5. Update File Syntax

### 5.1 Format

```text
*** Update File: src/app.ts
@@
-import oldThing from "./old"
+import newThing from "./new"

 function run() {
-   oldThing()
+  newThing()
 }
```

### 5.2 Hunk Structure

* A file update consists of one or more hunks.
* Each hunk begins with `@@`.
* Hunk content lines may be:
    * context lines: begin with a single space ` `
    * deletions: begin with `-`
    * additions: begin with `+`

### 5.3 Semantics

* Context lines must match the current file exactly.
* Deletion lines must match file content at the corresponding location.
* Addition lines insert new content.
* Multiple hunks apply in order.
* The file is updated only if all hunks validate and apply successfully.

### 5.4 Hunk Header Handling

The implementation must support hunks with:

* bare `@@`
* optional trailing text after `@@`

The trailing text, if present, should be treated as informational unless the parser requires it for anchoring.

### 5.5 Validation

* Reject update operations on missing files.
* Reject malformed hunk lines.
* Reject hunks that cannot be matched against current file contents.
* Reject patches with inconsistent line endings if policy requires it.
* Reject update bodies that appear to be full-file content without hunk markers unless explicitly supported.

## 6. Delete File Syntax

### 6.1 Format

```text
*** Delete File: obsolete.txt
```

### 6.2 Semantics

* Delete the file at the target path.
* No body content should follow.

### 6.3 Validation

* Reject if the file does not exist, unless idempotent delete is enabled.
* Reject if extra content follows the header.

## 7. Move Syntax

### 7.1 Format

Move is an optional sub-operation used with updates:

```text
*** Update File: src/old-name.ts
*** Move to: src/new-name.ts
@@
-oldName()
+newName()
```

### 7.2 Semantics

* Move the file from source path to destination path.
* If content changes are also present, apply them as part of the same logical file operation.
* If only `Move to` is present, rename without content changes.

### 7.3 Validation

* Reject if destination already exists, unless overwrite is allowed.
* Reject if the source file does not exist.
* Reject if `Move to` appears outside an update block.

## 8. Parsing Rules

### 8.1 General

The parser must process input line by line.

### 8.2 Required Behavior

* Recognize the begin and end markers.
* Recognize operation headers.
* Associate subsequent lines with the current operation.
* Preserve line order and exact text inside hunks and file bodies.

### 8.3 Error Handling

Parser errors must include:

* line number
* offending line
* reason for rejection

### 8.4 Unknown Content

* Content outside the envelope must be rejected.
* Unknown operation headers must be rejected.
* Unexpected body content after delete operations must be rejected.

## 9. Application Model

### 9.1 Atomicity

Default behavior must be atomic across the whole patch:

* Validate all operations first
* If any operation fails, apply none of them
* If all succeed, commit all changes

### 9.2 Application Order

Recommended application order:

1. Parse
2. Validate syntax
3. Validate filesystem preconditions
4. Resolve renames/moves
5. Apply contents
6. Commit changes

### 9.3 Conflict Policy

For update operations:

* Use exact matching by default
* Reject on first mismatch
* Report mismatch details for model recovery

## 10. Matching Algorithm for Updates

### 10.1 Required Behavior

Implement exact textual matching of hunk context and edit lines against current file contents.

### 10.2 Anchoring

* Context lines anchor the hunk.
* Deletion lines must be present at the matched location.
* Addition lines are inserted relative to the matched context.

### 10.3 Minimal Tolerance

The implementation may allow a small amount of syntactic flexibility in the patch text itself, but not in file matching, except where explicitly configured.

Examples of tolerated syntax variation:

* optional `@@` suffix text
* optional blank lines between hunks where unambiguous

Do not tolerate ambiguous structural deviations by default.

## 11. Filesystem Interface

The tool must operate against a workspace abstraction providing at least:

* `read(path) -> text`
* `write(path, text)`
* `delete(path)`
* `move(src, dst)`
* `exists(path) -> bool`

The implementation should support both disk-backed and in-memory workspaces.

## 12. Safety Requirements

The implementation must:

* prevent directory traversal
* reject unauthorized paths
* optionally protect files via policy
* avoid partial writes
* preserve file contents exactly where unchanged

## 13. Output Contract

The tool must return a structured result with at least:

* `status`: `completed` or `failed`
* `appliedOperations`: list of successful operations
* `failedOperation`: the first failed operation, if any
* `error`: human-readable explanation

Recommended failure example:

```text
status: failed
error: hunk context not found in src/app.ts at line 12
```

## 14. Reference Syntax Examples

### 14.1 Add File

```text
*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: notes.txt
+Hello
+World
*** End Patch
```

### 14.2 Update File

```text
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: src/main.py
@@
-print("Hi")
+print("Hello")
*** End Patch
```

### 14.3 Delete File

```text
*** Begin Patch
*** Delete File: old.txt
*** End Patch
```

### 14.4 Move File

```text
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: src/old.ts
*** Move to: src/new.ts
@@
-export const oldName = 1
+export const newName = 1
*** End Patch
```

## 15. Acceptance Criteria

An implementation is correct if it:

* parses valid patches matching the syntax above
* rejects malformed or unsafe patches
* supports add/update/delete/move
* applies updates with exact matching semantics
* applies patches atomically by default
* returns actionable error messages with line-level detail

## 16. Implementation Notes

* Keep the parser strict enough to avoid ambiguous interpretations.
* Keep the file application layer separate from parsing.
* Treat syntax and filesystem validation as distinct stages.
* Make error messages precise enough for an LLM to repair and retry.


## 17. References

This spec outlines the syntax used by OpenAI models and Codex and OpenCode's `apply_patch` tool. For additional details on syntax and behavior, reference:

* [OpenCode Tools](https://opencode.ai/docs/tools/) — OpenCode’s built-in tool docs, including `apply_patch` and its file-editing behavior.  
* [OpenCode File System Tools (DeepWiki)](https://deepwiki.com/opencode-ai/opencode/6.1-file-system-tools) — Detailed notes on OpenCode’s patch tool, validation, and permission flow.  
* [OpenAI Apply Patch Guide](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/tools-apply-patch) — Official OpenAI docs for structured file editing with `apply_patch`.  
* [OpenAI Apply Patch Guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-apply-patch) — Alternate OpenAI documentation page for the same tool, with examples and harness guidance.  
* [Codex Prompting Guide](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/gpt-5/codex_prompting_guide.md) — Includes the freeform patch grammar and implementation notes.  
* [Codex File Operations and Patch Application (DeepWiki)](https://deepwiki.com/openai/codex/6.3-configuration-management) — Implementation-oriented breakdown of Codex’s `apply_patch` tool, grammar, and handler architecture.  
* [Codex `ApplyPatchTool` API docs](https://hexdocs.pm/codex_sdk/Codex.Tools.ApplyPatchTool.html) — SDK-level docs showing usage, options, dry-run, and approval hooks.  
* [Codex CLI prompt instructions for `apply_patch`](https://fossies.org/linux/codex-rust/codex-rs/core/prompt_with_apply_patch_instructions.md) — Concrete patch syntax used in Codex CLI prompts.  
* [OpenAI Cookbook example: `apply_patch.py`](https://github.com/openai/openai-cookbook/blob/main/examples/gpt-5/apply_patch.py) — Reference implementation mentioned in the Codex prompting guide.  
* [OpenAI Agents SDK example: `apply_patch.py`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/main/examples/tools/apply_patch.py) — Example patch harness implementation for tool integration.

title: btw Addin cannot access R Environment / session objects (unlike `btw_app()`)
description:
### Summary

There is a functional discrepancy between launching the btw chat interface via the RStudio Addin vs. calling `btw_app()` directly: the Addin does not have access to the current R session environment, making `env` and `session` tools non-functional when used through the Addin.

### Expected behavior

The btw RStudio Addin should behave equivalently to `btw_app()` with respect to tool availability, including access to the current R environment and session objects (e.g., loaded data frames, model objects, defined variables).

### Actual behavior

When launching via the RStudio Addin:
- The tool selection UI correctly reflects the `btw.md` configuration (e.g., `tools: [docs, env, session]`)
- However, the `env` and `session` tools appear to have no access to the live R GlobalEnvironment — objects present in the session are not visible to the LLM

When launching via `btw_app()` in the console:
- Full access to the current R environment works as expected
- **However**, `btw_app()` blocks the R session, making parallel work in RStudio impossible

This creates a forced trade-off with no good solution:
- Addin → non-blocking, but no environment access
- `btw_app()` → environment access, but session is blocked



### Environment

```r
R version: 4.5.2
Platform: macOS (Apple Silicon)
RStudio version: 2026.4.0.347
btw version: 1.1.0
ellmer version: 0.4.0
```

### questions

- Could the Addin be modified to run in the same R process (or share environment state) rather than as a separate process?
- Alternatively, could `btw_app()` gain a `background = TRUE` argument that launches non-blocking (e.g., via `rstudioapi::jobRunScript()`) while retaining environment access?
- Or could environment snapshots be serialized and passed to the Addin process at launch time?

title: Feature Request: Auto-compact / Context Condensing for Long Conversations
description:
## Problem

When using `btw_app()` for extended iterative development sessions (e.g., writing code, running tests, fixing bugs in a loop), the input token count steadily grows — primarily due to accumulated tool call inputs/outputs (file reads, code search results, R execution output, etc.). Once it reaches ~200k tokens (the context window limit for models like Claude claude-4-opus), the API returns an input-too-long error and the conversation becomes unusable.

The only current workaround is to restart `btw_app()` and rely on `btw.md` to restore context, which breaks flow and loses nuanced conversation state (e.g., what approaches were already tried, intermediate debugging insights, implicit design decisions not captured in `btw.md`).

## Proposed Solution

Implement automatic context condensing (aka "auto-compact"), similar to what Claude Code and Cursor provide. The core idea:

1. **Monitor context size**: Track the current input token count (btw_app already displays this).
2. **Trigger condensing at a threshold**: When input tokens exceed a configurable percentage of the model's context window (e.g., 80%), automatically trigger a condensing step.
3. **Summarize conversation history**: Use the LLM itself to produce a structured summary of the conversation so far, preserving:
   - Current task and objectives
   - Files that have been created or modified (and key changes)
   - Design decisions made and their rationale
   - What has been tried and what failed
   - Pending next steps
4. **Replace old turns**: Use `Chat$set_turns()` to replace the full history with the condensed summary, freeing up token space for continued work.
5. **Continue seamlessly**: The user continues the conversation without interruption.

## Design Considerations

### Where should this live?

This could be implemented at either the **ellmer** or **btw** level:

- **ellmer level** (`Chat` class): A general-purpose `$condense()` method or an `auto_condense` option would benefit all ellmer-based applications. This is arguably the right abstraction layer since context window management is a fundamental chat concern.
- **btw level** (`btw_app()` / `btw_client()`): btw could implement this as a wrapper, using domain-specific summarization prompts optimized for coding conversations (files changed, tests passing/failing, etc.).

Both layers could work together — ellmer provides the mechanism, btw provides the coding-aware condensing prompt.

### Configurable options

```yaml
# In btw.md
condense:
  enabled: true
  threshold: 0.8          # Trigger at 80% of context window
  strategy: "summarize"   # or "truncate" for simpler approach
```

Or as R options:

```r
options(
  btw.condense = TRUE,
  btw.condense_threshold = 0.8
)
```

### Manual trigger

In addition to auto-triggering, a manual `/compact` command (or a button in `btw_app()`) would be valuable for users who want explicit control.

### What to preserve in the summary

For coding-focused conversations, the condensed summary should prioritize:

- **File state**: Which files were created/modified and what the key changes were
- **Task progress**: What's done, what's in progress, what's remaining
- **Failed approaches**: What was tried and didn't work (to avoid repeating mistakes)
- **Design decisions**: Architectural choices and their rationale
- **Current working context**: Which file/function the user was last working on

## Prior Art

- **Claude Code**: Implements auto-compact that triggers automatically when context grows large. Users can also type `/compact` to trigger manually.
- **Cursor**: Has "context condensation" that summarizes long conversations.
- **Aider**: Implements "chat summarization" to manage long coding sessions.
- **Continue.dev**: Provides conversation truncation strategies.

These tools demonstrate that context condensing is essentially a required feature for any coding agent used in long iterative sessions.

## Relation to Existing Issues

- **#66 (btw memory)**: Memory provides persistent cross-session facts, while condensing manages within-session conversation length. They are complementary — memory stores stable project knowledge, condensing manages ephemeral conversation history.
- **#148 (agentic btw_app sibling)**: A more agentic workflow will likely involve even longer sessions with more tool calls, making context condensing even more critical.

## My Use Case

I use `btw_app()` with Claude claude-4-opus for iterative R package development — writing functions, tests, documentation, then debugging and refining in a continuous loop. A typical productive session easily generates 200k+ tokens of context. Currently, I'm forced to restart every ~30-60 minutes, which significantly disrupts the development flow.

Context condensing would allow me to maintain continuous multi-hour development sessions without manual intervention.

title: is_text_file() rejects valid UTF-8 files with CJK text due to mid-character truncation at byte boundary
description:
`btw_tool_files_read()` incorrectly reports valid UTF-8 text files as binary when they contain dense CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean) characters. The root cause is that `is_text_file()` reads exactly 8192 bytes, which can split a multi-byte UTF-8 character at the buffer boundary, causing `validUTF8()` to return `FALSE`.

## Reprex

```r
# Create a Chinese-heavy UTF-8 text file where byte 8192 falls mid-character
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".txt")

# Each Chinese char = 3 bytes in UTF-8, so ~2731 chars = 8193 bytes
text <- paste(rep("测", 2731), collapse = "")
writeLines(text, tmp, useBytes = FALSE)

# Confirm the file is valid UTF-8
stopifnot(validUTF8(readLines(tmp, warn = FALSE)))

# But is_text_file() may reject it:
btw:::is_text_file(tmp)
# Returns FALSE (incorrectly) when the 8192-byte cut lands mid-character
```

Because 8192 is not divisible by 3 (the byte length of most CJK characters in UTF-8), there is a **2/3 probability** that any given CJK-heavy file hits this bug.

## Root Cause

The relevant code in `btw:::is_text_file()`:

```r
bytes <- readBin(con, what = "raw", n = 8192)
# ...
extended_chars <- bytes[bytes > as.raw(127)]
if (length(extended_chars) / length(bytes) > 0.3) {
  text <- rawToChar(bytes)
  if (Encoding(text) == "unknown" && !validUTF8(text)) {
    return(FALSE)
  }
}
```

The problem is a two-step interaction:

1. **`readBin(n = 8192)` truncates at an arbitrary byte offset.** UTF-8 characters can be 1–4 bytes long. For Chinese text (3-byte sequences), the 8192-byte cut has a 2/3 chance of landing inside a character. In the case I observed:

   | Byte position | Value  | Role                                      |
   |---------------|--------|-------------------------------------------|
   | 8191          | `0xe6` | Lead byte of 3-byte sequence (有, U+6709) |
   | 8192          | `0x9c` | Continuation byte (read — last byte in buffer) |
   | 8193          | `0x89` | Continuation byte (**not read, truncated**) |

2. **`validUTF8()` sees the incomplete trailing sequence `e6 9c` and returns `FALSE`.** The file is then misclassified as binary.

This branch is only entered when >30% of bytes are high bytes (>= 0x80), which is typical for dense CJK text (~73% in my case), so the bug specifically targets CJK-heavy files.

## Suggested Fix

Before calling `rawToChar()` + `validUTF8()`, trim any incomplete UTF-8 sequence from the end of the byte buffer:

```r
# Trim incomplete trailing UTF-8 sequence from the buffer
n <- length(bytes)
if (n > 0) {
  i <- n
  # Walk back at most 4 bytes (max UTF-8 char length) to find a lead byte
  while (i > 0 && i > n - 4) {
    b <- as.integer(bytes[i])
    if (b < 0x80) break                # ASCII byte — no truncation possible
    if (b >= 0xC0) {                   # Lead byte found
      needed <- if (b >= 0xF0) 4L else if (b >= 0xE0) 3L else 2L
      if (i + needed - 1L > n) {
        # Sequence is incomplete — trim it
        bytes <- bytes[1:(i - 1L)]
      }
      break
    }
    i <- i - 1L                        # Continuation byte — keep walking back
  }
}
```

title: `btw_tool_files_read_text_file()` fails to read valid UTF-8 files containing non-ASCII characters
description:
## Description

`btw_tool_files_read_text_file()` fails to read valid UTF-8 files containing non-ASCII characters (e.g., Cyrillic) on Windows with a non-English locale.

## Reproducible example
```r
# Create a file with Cyrillic characters
writeLines(c("# Тест", "1 + 1"), "test.R", useBytes = FALSE)

# This fails
btw::btw_tool_files_read_text_file("test.R")
#> Error: Path test.R is not a path to a text file.

# But the file is valid UTF-8
bytes  [1] TRUE
Encoding(text)
#> [1] "unknown"
```

## Root cause

In `is_text_file()`, line 
https://github.com/posit-dev/btw/blob/main/R/tool-files.R#L182
```r
if (Encoding(text) == "unknown" || !validUTF8(text)) {
    return(FALSE)
}
```

The condition uses `||` (OR), so even when `validUTF8()` returns `TRUE`, the file is rejected because `Encoding()` returns `"unknown"` on Windows.

## Suggested fix

Change `||` to `&&`:
```r
if (Encoding(text) == "unknown" && !validUTF8(text)) {
    return(FALSE)
}
```

This way, files are only rejected if the encoding is unknown **AND** they are not valid UTF-8.

## Session info

> ## Add a third-party MCP server (stdio) to VS Code
> 
> VS Code can run a local MCP server over **standard input/output (`stdio`)** by launching your provider’s executable (or a wrapper like `npx`, `python`, `uvx`, `docker`, etc.) from an `mcp.json` configuration.
> 
> ### Where to put the configuration
> 
> Pick one:
> 
> * **Workspace (recommended for team docs / per-project setup):** create `.vscode/mcp.json`
> * **User profile (global across projects):** Command Palette → **MCP: Open User Configuration** (opens your profile’s `mcp.json`)

title: Rename confusing tool groups and names
description:
There are a couple of [tool group names](https://posit-dev.github.io/btw/dev/reference/btw_tools.html) that I consistently find confusing when I haven't used them recently:

* `session`: I think this should be `sessioninfo` because it wraps functions from the sessioninfo package. I think I went with `session` because `sessioninfo` is redundant for `_package_info()` and `_platform_info()`, but those could be `_sessioninfo_package()` and `_sessioninfo_platform()`.

* `env`: I often confuse this with `session` (usually I think `session` means "give access to the current session" which is what `env` really is). Maybe this is fine if we rename `"session"`.

* `search`: Should be `"cran"`, e.g. `btw_tool_cran_package()` (for CRAN package info) and `btw_tool_cran_search()` to search on CRAN. This group could gain a tool for [CRAN Task Views](https://cran.r-project.org/web/views/).

* `files`: These tool names are overly verbose:
  * `btw_tool_files_code_search()` → `btw_tool_files_search()`
  * `btw_tool_files_list_files()` → `btw_tool_files_list()`
  * `btw_tool_files_read_text_file()` → `btw_tool_files_read()`
  * `btw_tool_files_write_text_file()` → `btw_tool_files_write()`

---

To effectuate this, we'd

1. For `btw_tools()` we support aliases, e.g. `btw_tools("session")` resolves to `btw_tools("sessioninfo")` or `btw_tools("files_read_text_file")` would resolve to `btw_tools("files_read")`:
   1. Add `alias_group` and `alias_name` properties to `.btw_add_to_tools()`
   2. During tool resolution, we'd match on `alias_group` and `alias_name` but emit a warning if matching to an alias occurs.
1. Update the tool function names and create alias function wrappers in `R/deprecated.R` that emit deprecation warnings using the `lifecycle` package.

title: Add `btw_tool_pkg_load_all()`
description:
# Feature Request: Implement `btw_tool_pkg_load_all()` tool

## Description
Implement a new tool `btw_tool_pkg_load_all()` that follows similar patterns to `btw_tool_pkg_test()` to run `pkgload::load_all()` but uses the `callr` package to run the code in a separate R process to avoid polluting the current R process.

## Motivation
The goal of `load_all()` as a tool is not to load the code in the current session, rather it's to:
- Confirm that the packaged code loads correctly (is free of syntax errors)
- If the package involves C, C++ or compilation in general, to cause re-compilation of that code

### Additional Use Cases from Agentic Coding Perspective

**Validation & Testing Workflow**
* Pre-test validation - Verify the package can load before running tests, catching load-time errors early
* Dependency checking - Confirm all package dependencies are available and can be loaded
* Namespace validation - Ensure NAMESPACE file is correctly configured and all exports/imports resolve

**Development Cycle Integration**
* Post-modification verification - After making code changes, quickly verify the package still loads without running full test suite
* Incremental development feedback - Get fast feedback on whether recent changes broke the package structure

**Debugging & Diagnostics**
* Error localization - Distinguish between load-time errors vs runtime errors
* Onload hook testing - Verify `.onLoad()` and `.onAttach()` functions execute correctly
* Collation order issues - Catch problems with file sourcing order specified in DESCRIPTION

**Agent Decision Making**
* Lighter than full check - Faster than `R CMD check` when you just need to verify loadability
* Prerequisite step - Natural first step before attempting to run examples or interactive testing
* Build system integration - Useful checkpoint in automated workflows before deploying or publishing

## Implementation Details
- Follow similar patterns to `btw_tool_pkg_test()`
- Use the `callr` package to run the code in a separate R process
- Avoid polluting the current R process

## Tool Instructions
The tool instructions should include a small instruction to use the run R code tool to call `load_all()` if the user needs the packaged code loaded in the current session.

title: a more agentic sibling to `btw_app()`
description:
Just jotting some notes down from an internal conversation. tl;dr: `btw_app()` should have a sibling with a more agentic, "Claude Code Dupe" feel.

As of now, [`side::kick()`](https://github.com/simonpcouch/side) is a separate package implementing something like this Claude Code Dupe idea:

* It has a `run_r_code()` and `bash()` tool that are registered automatically and, in most cases, do not require approval.
* It has more direct prompting about poise and feel that tell it to "just do stuff and say as little as possible."
* There's no setup flow other than installing the package--the app can discover providers and register them in a persistent way.

That said, `side::kick()` is quite scrappy and does all sorts of naughty namespacing tricks to make things happen. Because of this, 1) ellmer and shinychat and btw do not benefit when something gets implemented in side::kick(), and 2) side::kick() doesn't benefit when ellmer and shinychat and btw do things the right way.

These issues could be resolved by a sibling to `btw_app()` that is less configurable and more agentic, e.g. `btw::btw_agent()` or `btw::sidekick()` or otherwise. `btw_app()` can remain a more tailored-to-fit / safe interface to the suite of tools that btw provides.

title: FR: Auto-detect Quarto's bundled pandoc as fallback
description:
(Potential upstream issue.)

Hi folks.

I just ran into this error on a new laptop, whilst calling some of the `btw` help documentation tools (e.g., `btw_tool_docs_help_page`) from the CLI:

```
Mcp error: -32603: pandoc is required and was not found (see the help page ?rmarkdown::pandoc_available).
```

The error is obvious enough; I didn't have pandoc installed as a "standalone" binary and available on my PATH (via my package manager). OTOH it's not the full truth, since I _do_ have Quarto installed and this obviously bundles its own pandoc. I can imagine that other users are in a similar boat and this made me think that having a fallback option to / check for Quarto pandoc would be a useful feature.

What do you think about adding automatic detection of Quarto's bundled pandoc as a fallback when `rmarkdown::pandoc_available()` returns `FALSE`? Specifically, we could check common Quarto installation paths:

- macOS: `/Applications/quarto/bin/tools/pandoc`
- Windows: `~/AppData/Local/Programs/Quarto/bin/tools/pandoc` 
- Linux: `/opt/quarto/bin/tools/pandoc`

If found we could set `Sys.setenv(RSTUDIO_PANDOC = <path>)` to make it available to rmarkdown during this session?

title: New feature: GitHub API tool for repository and pull request information
description:
## Overview

This issue proposes a new tool to interface with the GitHub API, enabling btw to help users interact programmatically with GitHub repositories, issues, and pull requests.

## Scope

A new GitHub API tool would support querying repository information, listing and examining issues and pull requests, retrieving commit details, and other read-only operations. This would be useful for:

- Retrieving context about the current repository for project documentation
- Gathering information about open issues and PRs for code review or planning
- Comparing branches to understand what changed

## Proposed Endpoints

The planning document identifies three categories of endpoints to implement:

### Currently Implemented (Already Working)
- Issue and PR details, creation, and comments
- Search functionality

### High Confidence - Ready to Implement
- Repository details, branches, commits
- PR and issue metadata (reviews, timelines, events)
- Labels, milestones, checks, and status

### Moderate Confidence - Needs Review
- Branch creation/deletion, reviewer requests, assignees
- Reactions, releases, workflow runs
- Code and commit search
- File operations (create, update, delete)

### Not Recommended
- Repository settings, webhooks, merging, force push, deletion, secrets

## Endpoint Summary

| Category | Method | Endpoint | Purpose |
|----------|--------|----------|---------|
| Repository Info | GET | `/repos/{owner}/{repo}` | Get repository details |
| Branches | GET | `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches` | List all branches |
| Branches | GET | `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches/{branch}` | Get branch details |
| Contents | GET | `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/{path}` | Get file/directory contents |
| Commits | GET | `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits` | List commits |
| Commits | GET | `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits/{ref}` | Get commit details |
| Comparison | GET | `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/compare/{base}...{head}` | Compare branches/commits |
| PR Reviews | GET | `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pull_number}/reviews` | Get PR reviews |
| PR Commits | GET | `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pull_number}/commits` | Get PR commits |
| Issue Events | GET | `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{issue_number}/events` | Get issue events |
| Labels | GET | `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/labels` | List labels |
| Milestones | GET | `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/milestones` | List milestones |
| Status | GET | `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits/{ref}/status` | Get commit status |
| Checks | GET | `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits/{ref}/check-runs` | Get check runs |
| Update Issue | PATCH | `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{issue_number}` | Update issue |
| Update PR | PATCH | `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pull_number}` | Update PR |

## Next Steps

- [ ] Discuss endpoint selection with team
- [ ] Determine which endpoints to implement first
- [ ] Consider tool grouping and organization
- [ ] Plan integration with existing btw tools

title: Add `edit_btw_md()`
description:
Add a usethis-styled helper function to create and edit `btw.md` context files.

```r
edit_btw_md() # Create/edit `btw.md` in the current project root
edit_btw_md(scope = "project") # same
edit_btw_md(scope = "user") # Create/edit `~/btw.md`

edit_btw_md(scope = "path/to/btw.md") # create `btw.md` in a specified path
edit_btw_md(scope = "path/to") # same but assume `btw.md` as the filename
```

The function should create a default `btw.md` that looks something like this:

````markdown
---
client: claude/claude-4-5-sonnet-latest
tools: [docs, env, files, ide, search, session, web]
---

Follow these important style rules when writing R code:

* Prefer solutions that use {tidyverse}
* Always use `<-` for assignment
* Always use the native base-R pipe `|>` for piped expressions
````

Some thing for consideration:

* Could have `client` and `tools` arguments to pre-fill the YAML front matter. (This is immediately less relevant when `btw.md` already exists, so maybe not worth the complexity.)

* Could optionally not include the YAML front-matter if using `AGENTS.md`

* `edit_btw_md()` without arguments should follow the logic of `btw_client()`

* When creating a context file, `use_build_ignore(path)` to make sure it's ignored when building the R package

* Provides follow-up advice on how to customize the file
  * See `?btw_client` for info about the format
  * See `?btw_tools` for list of available tools
  * Use `btw_task_btw_init()` to create the initial context

title: Stale code search results after file writes
description:
If an agent calls `btw_tool_files_code_search`, then local state changes, then calls `btw_tool_files_code_search` again, the code search results are outdated.

``` r
library(btw)
library(ellmer)

test_dir <- withr::local_tempdir()

wd <- getwd()
setwd(test_dir)
withr::defer(setwd(wd))

dir.create(test_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

# finds line correctly at first:

title: btw_tools not quite compatible with Python agent frameworks
description:
Hi there, 

I have found an issue trying to use an MCP server with btw_tools together with various Python agent frameworks (e.g. [autogen](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/) ). I think the problem is in this line:

https://github.com/posit-dev/btw/blob/main/R/tools.R#L118

... where the `intent` argument is added as `.intent`. Tool wrappers in Python turn this into `_intent` since the dot at start isn't a valid Python parameter name and this makes the tool calls fail (I think). Of course this is technically not btw's fault but might still be easiest to fix here.

A minimal example can be constructed by running an MCP server as follows:

```bash
Rscript -e "mcptools::mcp_server(tools=btw::btw_tools())"
```

A basic autogen Python script to reproduce the error looks like this:

```python
# /// script
# dependencies = [
#   "autogen-agentchat",
#   "autogen-ext",
#   "openai",
#   "tiktoken",
#   "mcp",
#   "python-dotenv",
# ]
# ///

# Rscript -e "mcptools::mcp_server(tools=btw::btw_tools())"

import asyncio
import os

from autogen_agentchat.agents import AssistantAgent
from autogen_agentchat.teams import RoundRobinGroupChat
from autogen_agentchat.ui import Console
from autogen_ext.models.openai import OpenAIChatCompletionClient
from autogen_ext.tools.mcp import McpWorkbench, StdioServerParams
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()


async def main():
    """Main function to set up and run the AutoGen agent."""

    # Check if OpenAI API key is set
    if not os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"):
        print("Warning: OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable not set.")
        print("Please set your OpenAI API key before running this script.")
        print("Example: export OPENAI_API_KEY='your-api-key-here'")
        return 1

    # Create and start the assistant
    model_client = OpenAIChatCompletionClient(model="gpt-4.1")
    server_params = StdioServerParams(
        command="Rscript",
        args=[
            "-e",
            "mcptools::mcp_server(tools = btw::btw_tools())",
        ],
    )

    async with McpWorkbench(server_params) as mcp:
        agent = AssistantAgent(
            "r_assistant",
            model_client=model_client,
            workbench=mcp,
            model_client_stream=True,
            max_tool_iterations=10,
            reflect_on_tool_use=True,
            system_message="You are an R expert that helps the user answer questions about their R session.",
        )

        team = RoundRobinGroupChat([agent], max_turns=1)
        try:
            initial_task = input("What would you like to know about R? ")
            stream = team.run_stream(task=initial_task)
            await Console(stream, output_stats=True)
        except KeyboardInterrupt:
            print("\nConversation terminated by user.")

        # Clean up model client
        await model_client.close()

    return 0


def cli_main():
    """CLI entry point."""
    try:
        exit_code = asyncio.run(main())
        exit(exit_code)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        print("\nGoodbye!")
        exit(0)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    cli_main()

```

title: Review tool descriptions
description:
Tool descriptions are an important component, in particular for teaching the LLM how and when to correctly call the tool for best results. We should review and refine our tool definitions to make sure they're descriptive and effective. (But also tool definitions become tokens and contribute to the overall cost of the chat, so we should be careful not to be overly verbose.)

I asked Claude for best practices for tool definitions and descriptions and it provided this summary

> **Best Practices for LLM Tool Calling Optimization**
> 
> ## Naming and Description
> - Use clear, descriptive tool names that indicate functionality (e.g., "search_weather" instead of "get_data"). [^1]
> - Provide extremely detailed tool descriptions explaining exactly what the tool does, when to use it, and expected outputs. This is the most important factor for effective tool use. [^1]
> - Include examples of proper tool usage in descriptions when possible. [^2]
> 
> ## Parameters
> - Use descriptive parameter names that clearly indicate expected inputs. [^1]
> - Include detailed parameter descriptions explaining format, constraints, and examples. [^1]
> - Specify proper data types and constraints using JSON Schema to guide the LLM. [^3]
> - Consider renaming parameters to make their purpose more obvious to the model. [^2]
> 
> [^1]: https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/tool-use
> [^2]: https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents
> [^3]: https://community.aws/content/2hWA16FSt2bIzKs0Z1fgJBwu589/generating-json-with-the-amazon-bedrock-converse-api?lang=en

Anthropic’s [Best practices for tool definitions](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/tool-use#best-practices-for-tool-definitions) is also a good resource (found in the third link).
